audience.programmeDescription: International Land and Water Management combines natural science, social science and engineering to address drought, flooding, erosion and sustainable land use. Students study soils, water, farming and resource decisions through fieldwork, design and international professional experience.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR programmes respond through land, water, farming and environmental governance; quantitative and spatial environmental investigation; or policy, institutions and community inquiry. Dedicated hydraulics, irrigation, erosion-control engineering, integrated regional design and the required international placement remain important differences.

curriculum.limitation: This 180-credit example includes 117 prescribed taught credits, a 3-credit preparation choice for a Mathematics A entrant, an 18-credit internship and a concurrent 12-credit thesis, plus 30 open credits. The internship and thesis follow the required preparation, coordinator intake and safety training.

notes.text: WUR combines land and water science with hydraulic and irrigation design, farming, fieldwork, social inquiry, an international internship and a thesis. UCR develops substantial soil, water, climate, spatial, agricultural and governance interests, but does not reproduce the full specialist engineering, integrated regional-design and international-placement sequence. Optional UCR research is additional to each 180-credit schedule.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Personal & Professional Development
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Econometrics
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
